description: Scandinavian kingdom crystallised from the union of Svealand and Götaland (c. 980–1809) that dominated the Baltic region; its participation in the Kalmar Union (1397–1523) then liberation under Gustav Vasa marked Sweden's emergence as a sovereign power, while its control of Baltic iron and copper exports made it strategically important long before the seventeenth-century Swedish empire.

temporal.notes: Long Christianization; varying participation in Kalmar Union

lifecycle_phases.description: Olof Skötkonung (995–1022) is the first attested King of Sweden to be baptized a Christian and the first to rule both the Svear and the Götar peoples. Swedish Vikings (Varangians) dominate the eastern trade routes through Russia to Byzantium and Baghdad. Eric IX 'the Saint' (1156–1160) leads a crusade into Finland, beginning Swedish expansion eastward; his martyrdom makes him Sweden's patron saint.

The Folkunga dynasty under Birger Jarl (d. 1266) founds Stockholm (1252) and reforms governance. Magnus III (1275–1290) issues the first national law code. Birger II (1290–1318) is deposed by his brothers; Swedish governance is chronically unstable with competing noble factions. The Black Death (1350) and the temporary union under Magnus Eriksson with Norway creates complications before the Kalmar Union (1397) merges the Scandinavian kingdoms.

rise_factors.description: Swedish Varangian traders controlled the eastern routes through Russia, the Dnieper route to Byzantium and the Volga route to the Caspian, which were the main channels of eastern luxury goods to northern Europe; Stockholm's founding consolidated control of Baltic iron and copper exports

Swedish iron, copper, and timber were essential raw materials for the medieval European economy; Bergslagen's iron mines and Falun's copper mine gave Sweden structural economic leverage independent of military power

Swedish mines at Falun (copper) and Bergslagen (iron) produced metals in high demand across Europe; medieval Swedish kings taxed mining output and export trade, with the copper mine at Falun becoming one of the most important industrial enterprises in medieval Europe by the 14th century

Birka (then Sigtuna) connected Swedish territories to the Varangian trade routes through Russia; Swedish merchants sold furs, amber, and slaves to Byzantine and Arab buyers while importing silver that funded the royal court

Swedish kings and the Church formed a symbiotic alliance, kings provided military protection and land grants while bishops provided literacy, legal expertise, and legitimizing ceremony; the Archbishopric of Uppsala (1164) gave Sweden ecclesiastical independence from German churches

Sweden's Bergslagen mining district produced iron and copper that supplied Northern European markets; copper from Falun Mines in the 17th century provided over half of Europe's supply, funding Sweden's military expansion.

decline_factors.description: Swedish kingship was technically elective, with noble magnates repeatedly deposing kings; the struggle between the Folkunga dynasty branches and the eventual vacuum that allowed the Kalmar Union reflects the chronic weakness of royal authority against the Swedish nobility

The Kalmar Union (1397) formally united Scandinavia but in practice placed Sweden in a subordinate position to Danish kings; the repeated attempts by Swedish nobles to resist Danish domination (including Engelbrecht's rebellion, 1434) drained resources without achieving lasting independence until 1523

The Hanseatic League controlled Swedish foreign trade by the 14th century; Lübeck merchants dictated the price of Swedish copper, iron, and fish, capturing the trade surplus that could have funded royal centralization; the crown's inability to tax Hanseatic commerce was a structural fiscal weakness

Charles XII's catastrophic defeat at Poltava (1709) against Peter the Great's reformed Russian army ended the Swedish Empire's domination of the Baltic, triggering territorial losses that reduced Sweden to a secondary power.

sources.author: Sawyer, Birgit, and Sawyer, Peter
sources.title: Medieval Scandinavia: From Conversion to Reformation, circa 800–1500
